course.title: Corporate Finance: How Businesses Decide
course.description: How a company decides which projects to fund, how to pay for them and how much to give back to its owners, with a learner judging each choice rather than computing it.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read a balance sheet and income statement and has met compound interest, expected value and diversification. They want to judge whether a project, a borrowing, a payout or an acquisition makes sense, using Australian companies and tax where the sources allow.

paragraphs: How a company decides which projects to fund, how to pay for them and how much to give back to its owners, with a learner judging each choice rather than computing it.
outcomes: You'll be able to compare a payment now with a payment later and say what rate makes them equal.
You'll be able to say whether a project creates value, which cash flows belong in the answer, and when IRR or payback gives the wrong one.
You'll be able to explain what a required return is made of, what debt and equity each cost, and why a project needs a rate that matches its own risk.
You'll be able to judge whether a firm should borrow more, pay out cash or buy back shares, and say what a franked dividend is worth to a given shareholder.
You'll be able to find the assumption an answer depends on and check a forecast against what happened to similar projects.
You'll be able to say whether an acquisition price can pay off and what a share price can and cannot tell a manager.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Accounting: Reading the Numbers of a Business, Personal Finance and Investing, Economics: Markets and Strategy, Decision Theory, Maths Foundations.

modules.title: Time and value
modules.description: Money now and money later: why waiting has a price, how to turn a stream of future cash into a value today, and where the value of a long stream sits.

modules.title: Choosing projects
modules.description: Use net present value to decide whether a project creates value, decide which cash flows belong in it, and know when IRR and payback mislead.

modules.title: The cost of capital
modules.description: Where the discount rate comes from: what investors require for risk, what debt and equity each cost, and how a firm's blended rate and a project's own rate differ.

modules.title: Financing and paying out
modules.description: Why firms borrow, when borrowing costs more than it saves, and how they decide between keeping cash, paying dividends and buying back shares, with Australia's franking credits.

modules.title: Uncertainty, deals and markets
modules.description: Which assumption an answer hinges on, whether an acquisition price can pay off, and what a share price does and does not tell a manager.

concepts.title: Time value of money
concepts.summary: Money in hand can be invested, so the same sum is worth more now than later.

concepts.title: Discount rate
concepts.summary: The return given up by waiting: what the same money would earn in the best alternative of the same risk.

concepts.title: Present value
concepts.summary: The value today of money due later, found by discounting it at the discount rate.

concepts.title: Break-even rate
concepts.summary: The rate at which waiting and not waiting are worth the same; below it waiting wins, above it taking the money now wins.

concepts.title: Annuity
concepts.summary: A series of equal payments at regular intervals.

concepts.title: Perpetuity
concepts.summary: Payments that continue forever; with a steady payment its value is the payment divided by the rate.

concepts.title: Terminal value
concepts.summary: The value placed on all cash flows after the years that are forecast in detail; often a large share of a valuation.

concepts.title: Rate sensitivity
concepts.summary: The further out a payment is, the more a change in the discount rate moves its present value.

concepts.title: Net present value
concepts.summary: The present value of a project's cash flows less its cost: the value it adds, in today's dollars, over what investors could earn elsewhere.

concepts.title: Required return (hurdle rate)
concepts.summary: The return investors could earn on other investments of the same risk; the discount rate in an NPV.

concepts.title: Independent projects
concepts.summary: Projects that can all be undertaken if each adds value and capital is not short; their NPVs add.

concepts.title: Zero NPV
concepts.summary: A project that earns exactly the required return: it neither adds nor loses value.

concepts.title: Incremental cash flow
concepts.summary: Cash that changes because the project goes ahead, compared with the firm without it.

concepts.title: Sunk cost
concepts.summary: Money already spent or committed that cannot be recovered whatever is decided; it stays out.

concepts.title: Opportunity cost
concepts.summary: The best use of an owned asset that the project gives up; it counts even though no cash is paid out.

concepts.title: Side effect
concepts.summary: A change to the firm's other products or costs caused by the project, including lost sales of existing products.

concepts.title: Working capital as a cash flow
concepts.summary: Stock, receivables and cash floats tie up cash at the start and release it at the end.

concepts.title: Internal rate of return
concepts.summary: The discount rate at which a project's NPV is zero: the return it earns.

concepts.title: Payback period
concepts.summary: The time taken for a project's cash flows to repay its cost; it ignores timing and what comes after.

concepts.title: Mutually exclusive projects
concepts.summary: Projects of which at most one can be undertaken, such as two designs for the same site.

concepts.title: Multiple IRRs
concepts.summary: A project whose cash flows change sign more than once can have more than one IRR, or none that make sense.

concepts.title: Risk-free rate
concepts.summary: The return on an investment assumed to meet every payment, usually a government bond in the same currency; the base of every required return.

concepts.title: Risk premium
concepts.summary: The extra return investors demand for cash flows that may not arrive.

concepts.title: Systematic and firm-specific risk
concepts.summary: Systematic risk is common to all shares and cannot be diversified away; firm-specific risk can, so the market does not pay for it.

concepts.title: Beta
concepts.summary: How much a share tends to move with the market as a whole; the average share has a beta of 1.

concepts.title: Cost of debt
concepts.summary: What lenders require on new borrowing today: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the chance of default, less the value of the interest deduction.

concepts.title: Cost of equity
concepts.summary: What shareholders require: the risk-free rate plus a premium for the risk they carry; no contract promises it, but it is a cost all the same.

concepts.title: Priority of claims
concepts.summary: Lenders are paid before shareholders, who receive what is left, which may be nothing.

concepts.title: Leverage raises the cost of equity
concepts.summary: More debt leaves shareholders with a riskier residual, so they require more.

concepts.title: Weighted average cost of capital
concepts.summary: The blend of what lenders and shareholders require, weighted by the market value of each and with interest taken after tax; set by the market, not by management.

concepts.title: Hurdle rate
concepts.summary: The return a project must beat; for a project like the rest of the firm it can be the WACC, otherwise it should match the project's own risk.

concepts.title: Project-specific rate
concepts.summary: A required return based on the systematic risk of the project, found from firms in the same line of business or by adjusting the WACC up or down.

concepts.title: WACC is an estimate
concepts.summary: Each input has several plausible proxies, so a fairly wide range of values can look defensible.

concepts.title: Financial leverage
concepts.summary: Borrowing to fund assets so that owners' return rises when the assets earn more than the debt costs, and falls further when they earn less.

concepts.title: Tax shield
concepts.summary: The tax saved because interest is deductible while dividends are not.

concepts.title: Modigliani-Miller without taxes
concepts.summary: In a perfect market with no taxes or distress costs, the mix of debt and equity does not change firm value.

concepts.title: Dividend imputation
concepts.summary: Company tax is passed to shareholders as a credit, so profit paid to eligible shareholders is taxed at their own rate.

concepts.title: Financial distress
concepts.summary: A condition in which promises to creditors are broken or honoured with difficulty; it has direct costs (fees) and indirect costs (higher interest, lost attention, lost projects).

concepts.title: Trade-off theory
concepts.summary: Firms balance the tax benefit of debt against the cost of bankruptcy and distress.

concepts.title: Interest cover
concepts.summary: Profit before interest divided by the interest bill: how many times the interest could be paid out of profit.

concepts.title: Debt overhang
concepts.summary: Existing debt so large that the firm cannot take on a good new investment because the gains would go to lenders.

concepts.title: Pecking order
concepts.summary: Firms prefer internal funds, then debt, and raise equity last, because outsiders read a share issue as bad news.

concepts.title: Payout ratio
concepts.summary: Dividends as a share of earnings (or of free cash flow); above 100% means paying out more than was earned.

concepts.title: Residual dividend policy
concepts.summary: Invest in every project that beats the required return, then pay out what is left.

concepts.title: Share buyback
concepts.summary: The company buys its own shares; earnings per share rise because there are fewer shares.

concepts.title: Franking credit
concepts.summary: A credit for company tax already paid, passed on with a dividend; usable by eligible Australian taxpayers, refundable to some.

concepts.title: Signalling
concepts.summary: A rise in the dividend, or a buyback, may tell the market that management is confident or thinks the shares are cheap.

concepts.title: Sensitivity analysis
concepts.summary: Changing one input at a time to see how far the answer moves; it shows which forecasts deserve effort.

concepts.title: Break-even input
concepts.summary: The value of an assumption at which NPV is zero.

concepts.title: Scenario analysis
concepts.summary: Changing linked inputs together, such as price and volume.

concepts.title: Outside view (reference class forecasting)
concepts.summary: Forecasting from the outcomes of similar past projects instead of from the details of this one.

concepts.title: Planning fallacy
concepts.summary: The tendency to underestimate time, cost and risk and overestimate benefits.

concepts.title: Control premium
concepts.summary: The amount a buyer pays over the market price to gain control of a listed company.

concepts.title: Synergy
concepts.summary: A benefit a buyer expects from combining the businesses; cost synergies are trusted more than revenue synergies.

concepts.title: Winner's curse
concepts.summary: In a contest where all bidders value the prize about the same, the winner is the one with the most optimistic estimate, and so tends to overpay.

concepts.title: Managerial overconfidence
concepts.summary: Managers overrate the synergies, and so overpay.

concepts.title: Efficient-market hypothesis
concepts.summary: Prices reflect all available information, so prices move only on new information and nobody can consistently beat the market on a risk-adjusted basis.

concepts.title: Surprise
concepts.summary: Only the part of news that differs from what was expected moves the price.

concepts.title: Weak, semi-strong and strong forms
concepts.summary: The information in question is past prices, all public information, or private information as well.

concepts.title: Event study
concepts.summary: Reading the effect of an event on a firm's value from its share price around the event.

lessons.title: Money now and money later
lessons.orientation: Compare a payment now with a larger payment later by asking what the money could earn elsewhere, and say which is worth more and at what rate the answer flips.

lessons.title: Value that arrives late
lessons.orientation: Judge how much of a long cash stream's value arrives in the early years and how much far out, and say which streams a change in the discount rate hurts most.

lessons.title: Net present value
lessons.orientation: Decide whether a project creates value by comparing its cost with the present value of what it returns at the rate investors require, and read the answer as value added today.

lessons.title: Which cash flows count
lessons.orientation: Sort the items in a project proposal into the cash flows that belong in its NPV and those that do not: sunk costs, opportunity costs, side effects, working capital, tax and financing costs.

lessons.title: IRR and payback: where they mislead
lessons.orientation: Compare projects by NPV, IRR and payback, say which rule to trust when they disagree, and spot the cases where IRR or payback gives the wrong answer.
lessons.reviewLabel: IRR and payback: where they mislead

lessons.title: Risk and required return
lessons.orientation: Explain why riskier cash flows are discounted at higher rates, separate the risk investors are paid for from the risk they can remove by holding many shares, and rank businesses by how much they move with the economy.

lessons.title: What debt and equity cost
lessons.orientation: Say why a firm's debt costs less than its equity, why that does not make borrowing cheap overall, and where each cost comes from.

lessons.title: WACC and hurdle rates
lessons.orientation: Say what WACC measures, what raises or lowers it, and why a project should be judged at a rate that matches its own risk rather than the company's average.

lessons.title: Why firms borrow
lessons.orientation: Judge what borrowing does to the return and risk of a firm's owners, and say how the tax treatment of interest, and of dividends in Australia, changes the case for debt.

lessons.title: Distress and the trade-off
lessons.orientation: Judge whether a firm should borrow more by weighing the tax benefit of debt against the costs of financial distress, given how steady its cash flows are.

lessons.title: Dividends, buybacks and franking credits
lessons.orientation: Judge whether a firm should pay cash out or keep it, whether to use a dividend or a buyback, and what a franked dividend is worth to different shareholders.

lessons.title: Forecasts and sensitivity
lessons.orientation: Find which assumption a project's value hinges on, work out how far it can move before the answer flips, and judge a forecast against what happened to similar projects.

lessons.title: Acquisitions and the price paid
lessons.orientation: Judge whether an acquisition price can pay off by comparing the premium with the synergies the buyer can realistically deliver, and say how competition and overconfidence push buyers to overpay.

lessons.title: What a share price tells you
lessons.orientation: Judge from a piece of news whether a share price should move, say what the efficient-market idea does and does not claim, and decide what a manager can and cannot read from the market's price.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a share price tells you
